backend.concurrency.race_conditions.rationale: Shared-memory multithreading makes data races a routine bug class in Java, Go, C and C++, which have formal memory models and race detectors (JMM, go race detector, TSan). Rust prevents data races at compile time, so only logic races remain. Single-threaded Node and shared-nothing PHP mostly see check-then-act races across awaits or concurrent requests hitting the database, so they sit at 0.4.

backend.concurrency.locking_and_lock_ord.rationale: Explicit mutexes and lock-ordering rules are everyday material in Java (synchronized/ReentrantLock), Go (sync.Mutex), C (pthreads) and C++ (std::lock, Abseil), with CERT rules on lock order for C and Java. Rust, C#, Kotlin and Python have first-class locks too. Scala idioms (actors, Ref) avoid locks. In JS/TS, Ruby and PHP, locking mostly means DB row locks or Redis/cache locks.

backend.concurrency.deadlocks.rationale: Lock-order deadlocks are canonical in Java, C and C++. Go has channel/goroutine deadlocks ('all goroutines are asleep'). C# has the well-known sync-over-async (.Result/.Wait) deadlock. Kotlin (runBlocking), Scala (blocking Await on a bounded pool) and Python (threading, asyncio) have their own variants. In JS/TS, Ruby and PHP, deadlocks mostly appear as database transaction deadlocks.

backend.concurrency.thread_and_worker_po.rationale: Java (ThreadPoolExecutor), C# (ThreadPool starvation) and Python (concurrent.futures, gunicorn/Celery workers) are mainstream homes of pool sizing and queueing bugs. Go worker pools, Ruby Puma/Sidekiq concurrency, tokio spawn_blocking, Kotlin dispatchers and Scala ExecutionContexts are common. Node's worker_threads/libuv pool and PHP-FPM pm settings are plausible but less code-level.

backend.concurrency.async_await_pitfalls.rationale: async/await is native and pervasive in TS/JS, Python (asyncio), C# and Rust (tokio), each with canonical pitfalls: floating promises, blocking the event loop, async void, holding locks across await. Kotlin coroutines and Scala Futures are close equivalents. Java has only CompletableFuture (and virtual threads), Go uses goroutines instead of async/await, Ruby and PHP async ecosystems (async gem, Fibers/ReactPHP) are niche, and C has nothing comparable.

backend.concurrency.atomic_operations.rationale: Atomics with memory orderings are first-class in C11, C++ std::atomic, Rust std::sync::atomic, Go sync/atomic and java.util.concurrent.atomic. C# has Interlocked and Kotlin has JVM atomics. Scala usually wraps them (AtomicReference, cats-effect Ref). Python and Ruby have no userland atomics, JS Atomics only apply to SharedArrayBuffer, and PHP has none.

backend.concurrency.shared_state_in_requ.rationale: Mutable fields on singleton Spring beans, ASP.NET singleton services capturing scoped state, and Go handlers running concurrently on one goroutine per request are classic bugs. Node module-level state leaks across requests, and Rails/Puma and Python module globals are common too. Rust forces Arc<Mutex> so only logic bugs remain, C/C++ are rarely written as request handlers, and PHP-FPM is shared-nothing (only Octane/Swoole worker mode reintroduces it).

backend.resilience.timeouts.rationale: Missing or mis-propagated timeouts are a universal backend bug. C++ infrastructure (gRPC, Envoy) deals with deadlines constantly. Plain C service code is less common.

backend.resilience.retries_and_backoff.rationale: Well-known retry libraries define the 1.0s: resilience4j/Failsafe (Java), Polly and Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience (C#), cenkalti/backoff (Go), tenacity (Python). Node (p-retry), Ruby (retriable, Sidekiq retries), Rust (backoff, tower), Scala (ZIO Schedule) and PHP (Laravel retry/queue backoff) have common support. C rarely hosts this logic, and in C++ it lives mostly in gRPC internals.

backend.resilience.rate_limiting.rationale: Token-bucket limiters are standard library or framework level in Go (x/time/rate) and Java (resilience4j, Guava, Bucket4j). backend.resilience.graceful_degradation.rationale: Fallbacks and load shedding are architectural and fairly language-neutral. C++ (RocksDB, many storage engines) and C (PostgreSQL's MVCC itself) count for infrastructure, but C exercises would be engine-internals only.

Twelve-factor guidance on keeping credentials out of code

backend.security.session_and_token_handl.rationale: Node (express-session, jsonwebtoken), Java (JJWT/Spring) and PHP (native sessions) are where session/JWT validation mistakes are most discussed; OWASP's JWT and session cheat sheets centre on these stacks. Python, Ruby, C# and Go have standard libraries (PyJWT, Rails cookie store, golang-jwt), while C/C++ rarely implement web sessions.

sources.supports: OWASP session management pitfalls (fixation, expiry, cookie flags)
OWASP JWT cheat sheet (signature validation, algorithm confusion, revocation)
jsonwebtoken: the dominant Node.js JWT library
express-session: standard session middleware for Node
golang-jwt: the standard Go JWT library
PyJWT: the standard Python JWT library

backend.observability.structured_logging.rationale: Go ships structured logging in the standard library (log/slog), C# has Serilog's message templates, and Java has MDC plus JSON encoders; these are routine. Python (structlog), Node (pino) and Rust (tracing) are common; Ruby, PHP (Monolog context) and C++ (spdlog) are thinner, and C services usually log plain text.

sources.supports: Rust tracing crate with structured fields
Monolog: PHP logging with context arrays

backend.observability.metrics.rationale: Prometheus' official clients are Go, Java/Scala, Python, Ruby, Rust and Node; Go and Java (Micrometer) are the mainstream homes of metric instrumentation bugs (cardinality, counter vs gauge). C++ infrastructure (Envoy) is metric-heavy; C, Ruby and PHP rely on thinner or third-party support (PHP's shared-nothing model needs external storage).

sources.supports: Official Prometheus clients: Go, Java/Scala, Python, Ruby, Rust, Node; C, C++, .NET and PHP third-party
Micrometer: the JVM metrics facade used by Spring Boot
OpenTelemetry metrics stability per language (Kotlin and Ruby metrics still in development)

backend.observability.tracing.rationale: OpenTelemetry tracing is stable and widely deployed in Java, Go and .NET (where context propagation bugs are a routine topic); Python, Node, C++ (Envoy) and Rust (tracing crate) are common. Ruby and PHP have stable SDKs but less usage, Kotlin uses the JVM SDK, and C has essentially no mainstream tracing SDK.

sources.supports: OpenTelemetry per-language status (traces stable for C++, .NET, Go, Java, JS, PHP, Python, Ruby; Rust beta; no C SDK)

backend.observability.health_checks.rationale: Spring Boot Actuator and ASP.NET Core health checks are built-in frameworks for liveness/readiness, and Go is the home of Kubernetes probes and the gRPC health protocol. Other web stacks add a handler by hand; C/C++ infrastructure exposes admin endpoints but rarely as a reading exercise topic.

sources.supports: Spring Boot Actuator health endpoint and indicators (Java/Kotlin)
Envoy admin interface health endpoints (C++ infrastructure)

backend.observability.logging_sensitive_.rationale: Logging whole request objects or entities (Java toString, Kotlin data classes) and request params is a canonical leak; Rails has filter_parameters for exactly this. Rust (derived Debug) and Scala (case class toString) can leak too but it is less discussed; C/C++ services rarely log user payloads.

sources.supports: OWASP logging cheat sheet: data to exclude from logs (passwords, tokens, PII)
Rails configuration including filter_parameters to mask sensitive params in logs
Twitter 2018: a bug wrote plaintext passwords to an internal log (GitHub had a similar incident days earlier)

backend.config.configuration_loading.rationale: Spring Boot's externalized configuration and .NET's layered configuration providers make precedence/binding bugs routine; Go's Viper is the standard for services and CLIs. Python (pydantic-settings), Node and Rust (config + serde) are common; Ruby/PHP frameworks hide most loading, and C/C++ infra parses config files by hand (PostgreSQL, Abseil flags).

sources.supports: Spring Boot externalized configuration and property source ordering
ASP.NET Core configuration providers and precedence

backend.config.feature_flags.rationale: Feature-flag SDKs (OpenFeature, LaunchDarkly, Unleash) cover all mainstream web languages, so most are common; Ruby gets 1.0 for Flipper and the Rails culture of flag-gated rollouts. Rust and Scala have thinner SDK support, C++ infrastructure uses runtime flags (Envoy), and C rarely has them.

backend.config.environment_specific_beha.rationale: Rails environments, Spring profiles and ASP.NET Core environments are framework features where dev/prod divergence bugs are routine; Django settings, NODE_ENV and Laravel APP_ENV are common. Go and Rust have no framework convention (env vars, build tags, cfg), and C/C++ mostly see it as #ifdef/NDEBUG differences.

sources.supports: Twelve-factor: config that varies between deploys belongs in the environment

backend.config.defaults_and_validation.rationale: Python (pydantic-settings), .NET (options validation) and Spring (@ConfigurationProperties with @Validated) have first-class typed config validation; Go's zero values and envconfig defaults, Rust's serde defaults and zod in Node are common settings. Ruby, PHP, Scala and C/C++ do it ad hoc.

sources.supports: pydantic-settings: typed settings with defaults and validation
envconfig: Go env config with defaults and required fields
zod: schema validation commonly used for env/config in TypeScript
serde: Rust deserialization with field defaults

backend.testing.unit_test_design.rationale: Every mainstream backend language has a standard test framework (JUnit, pytest, Go testing, xUnit/NUnit, RSpec, Jest, cargo test, GoogleTest, ScalaTest, PHPUnit), so most score high; the 1.0s have the strongest test-design culture and literature. C has thin, fragmented frameworks.

backend.testing.mocking_and_fakes.rationale: Mocking libraries are central in Java (Mockito), Kotlin (MockK), C# (Moq), Python (unittest.mock) and JS/TS (Jest), where over-mocking and wrong-patch-target bugs are routine. Go favours hand-written fakes behind interfaces (gomock exists); Rust (mockall) and C++ (gMock) need trait/virtual seams, and C has little support.

backend.testing.flaky_tests.rationale: The main empirical flaky-test study is on Apache (Java) projects, with async waits, concurrency and test-order dependency as the top causes; these causes arise in every language with async/concurrent tests (Node async, Go goroutines, RSpec random order). Rust's ownership rules and C/C++/PHP's smaller test cultures make it less common as an exercise.

sources.supports: Luo et al., An Empirical Analysis of Flaky Tests (FSE 2014): 51 Apache projects; async wait, concurrency, order dependency
Google Testing Blog: flaky tests at Google and mitigation
Go race detector, a common tool for timing-dependent test failures

backend.testing.integration_tests.rationale: Java (Spring Boot tests, Testcontainers' origin) and Rails (integration/system tests built into the framework) are the canonical homes; Testcontainers modules for Go, .NET, Node, Python plus Django/Laravel test clients make the others common. Rust and C++ have thinner tooling, and C rarely has service-level integration suites.

sources.supports: Testcontainers: Java, Go, .NET, Node.js, Python, Rust and other implementations
Rails testing guide: integration and system tests
Django testing tools (test client, database setup)

backend.design.dependency_injection.rationale: DI containers are core framework features in Java (Spring), C# (Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection), TypeScript (NestJS), PHP (Laravel's service container) and Kotlin (Koin, Spring, Dagger). Go (Wire, fx, constructor injection), Python (FastAPI Depends) and Scala (ZIO layers) are common; Ruby/JS lean on duck typing and module patching, and C rarely uses it.

backend.design.layering.rationale: Controller/service/repository layering is the default architecture in Spring and ASP.NET (with official guidance), and common in Nest, Django, Rails, Laravel and Go services. Plain JS, Rust, Scala and C/C++ code is less often organised around these layers, so violations look less natural.

sources.supports: Microsoft guide to layered and clean architectures for .NET web apps
Spring stereotypes (@Controller/@Service/@Repository) encode layering in Java

backend.design.interface_design.rationale: Explicit abstractions are central in Go (small implicit interfaces), Rust (traits), Java and C#; TypeScript, Kotlin, Scala, C++ and PHP interfaces/abstract classes are common. Python, Ruby and JS rely on duck typing (Protocols are optional), and C uses headers and function-pointer tables, so interface-design exercises are plausible but less natural there.

sources.supports: Rust book: traits as shared behaviour

backend.design.coupling_and_cohesion.rationale: Largely language-neutral, but most discussed in large Java and C# codebases (OO design literature, DI-based decoupling). It is a common reading topic in the other mainstream backend languages and C++; Rust, Scala and C have smaller corpora of service code organised this way.

sources.supports: Refactoring catalog (Move Function, Extract Class, etc.) for coupling and cohesion

backend.design.code_duplication.rationale: Copy-paste is language-neutral (PMD CPD detects it across most of these languages). Go gets 1.0 because it lacked generics until 1.18 and duplicated code is a well-known idiom cost there; C is also prone because it has no generics. Rust, C++ and Scala have strong abstraction tools (generics, macros, templates), so duplication is less often the point of an exercise.

sources.supports: PMD copy-paste detector, supporting most mainstream languages
Go blog: generics introduced to avoid writing the same code per type
Refactoring catalog: Extract Function and related duplication fixes

backend.distributed.sharding_and_partiti.rationale: Partitioning logic lives mostly in infrastructure: Kafka/Cassandra/Elasticsearch (Java), Vitess/CockroachDB (Go), ScyllaDB/MongoDB (C++), TiKV (Rust), Redis Cluster hash slots (C), Akka Cluster Sharding (Scala). App stacks (Rails horizontal sharding, Django routers) make it plausible elsewhere; PHP rarely.

sources.supports: Ruby: application-level horizontal sharding exists but is less central.

backend.distributed.replication_and_cons.rationale: Consensus implementations engineers actually read are etcd/raft and hashicorp/raft (Go), ZooKeeper/Kafka KRaft (Java), raft-rs/TiKV (Rust), braft (C++) and canonical/raft (C). Scala via Akka Cluster/Kafka. In TS/JS/Python/Ruby/PHP backends this is library-consumer territory, so code-reading exercises would look contrived.

sources.supports: Go: HashiCorp Raft used by Consul/Nomad/Vault.

backend.distributed.cross_service_consis.rationale: Sagas and transactional outbox are microservice patterns with strong library support in Java (Debezium outbox, Axon/Eventuate), C# (MassTransit sagas and outbox) and Go (Temporal server, common in Go microservices); TS/Python/Kotlin/Scala are natural settings. Ruby/PHP monoliths meet it less, and C/C++ rarely.

sources.supports: Go: Temporal durable workflow engine (SDKs in Go/Java/TS/Python/.NET).

backend.performance.profiling_and_hot_pa.rationale: Hot-path tuning is routine in C/C++/Rust infrastructure (perf, flame graphs), Go (pprof built in) and Java (async-profiler, JMH). Python (py-spy), C# (dotnet-trace), Node (--prof), Ruby (stackprof) and the JVM languages have well-known profilers. PHP has Xdebug/Blackfire/Tideways, but request-scoped PHP code is less often tuned at the hot-loop level.

sources.supports: Flame graphs for CPU profiling (perf, many runtimes)

backend.integrations.webhooks_outbound.rationale: Sending webhooks (retries, signing, timeouts, SSRF) is product-API work: TS/Node and Ruby (Rails SaaS) are the typical homes, with dedicated dispatchers like Svix (Rust) and Convoy (Go) and spatie/laravel-webhook-server for PHP. C/C++ services essentially never send webhooks.

sources.supports: Cross-language spec for signing/delivering webhooks, with libraries in many languages.
Rust: Svix webhook delivery server; SDKs for many languages.
PHP: outbound webhooks with retries and signing for Laravel.

backend.integrations.third_party_adapter.rationale: Wrapping payment/email/CRM APIs is glue work; vendors like Stripe ship official SDKs for Node, Python, Ruby, PHP, Java, Go and .NET, and Resilience4j/Polly exist for the retry/timeout wrapping. Kotlin/Scala/Rust get unofficial or JVM SDKs, and C/C++ backends rarely integrate SaaS APIs.

sources.supports: Official server SDK languages for a major third-party API.
Java: resilience library for wrapping remote calls.
C#: Polly retry/circuit-breaker for external calls.

backend.data.nosql_modeling.rationale: Document and single-table modeling is most at home in Node/TS (Mongoose, ElectroDB for DynamoDB), with Java (Spring Data MongoDB, DynamoDB Enhanced Client), Python (boto3/pymongo), Go and C# (Cosmos DB) common. Ruby/PHP stacks lean on relational ORMs; C/C++ only appear as the database engine, not as data-model code.

sources.supports: C#/.NET ecosystem: Cosmos DB data modeling.

backend.data.money_and_ledgers.rationale: Java (BigDecimal, JSR 354/Moneta), C# (built-in decimal), Python (decimal) and Ruby (BigDecimal plus the money gem) have first-class decimal money types and many fintech codebases. JS/TS make the float-rounding bug canonical but need Dinero.js-style libraries; Go uses shopspring/decimal; Rust has rust_decimal; C++ appears in trading (fixed-point); C rarely.

sources.supports: Java: JSR 354 Money and Currency reference implementation.
Python: decimal module with rounding control.
JS/TS: immutable money library to avoid float errors.

backend.security.audit_logging.rationale: Mature audit libraries make it routine in Ruby (PaperTrail) and Java (Hibernate Envers); Go has Kubernetes API audit logging, and the other web stacks implement audit trails with ORM hooks. C appears via pgaudit, while Rust, Scala and C++ rarely centre on it.

sources.supports: OWASP: which security events to record in audit logs
PaperTrail: model change auditing for Rails
Hibernate Envers: entity auditing for Java

backend.security.encryption_at_rest_and_.rationale: C (OpenSSL), Go (crypto/tls in the stdlib) and Java (JCA/JSSE) are the mainstream homes of TLS configuration and cipher-misuse bugs; Rust (rustls), C++, Python (cryptography), .NET, Rails (Active Record encryption) and PHP (sodium, Laravel encryption) are common. Node services usually terminate TLS elsewhere and use node:crypto less often.

sources.supports: OpenSSL: the C TLS/crypto library underlying much infrastructure

backend.security.multi_tenant_isolation.rationale: Ruby (acts_as_tenant, Apartment) and C# (EF Core global query filters, official multi-tenancy guidance) have first-class tenant-scoping patterns where a missing filter is the canonical bug; Python (django-tenants), Java (Hibernate) and Node/Go SaaS backends are common. C/C++ backends almost never implement tenant scoping in application code (it lives in the database, e.g. PostgreSQL RLS).

sources.supports: EF Core multi-tenancy guidance (global query filters, per-tenant databases)
acts_as_tenant: row-level tenant scoping for Rails
PostgreSQL row-level security, often used for tenant isolation at the DB layer

backend.realtime.connection_fanout.rationale: Broadcasting to many WebSocket clients is the core use case of Node (socket.io rooms, Redis adapter, ws) and Go (gorilla/websocket hub). It is common in Java (Spring STOMP), C# (SignalR backplanes), Python (Django Channels groups), Ruby (Action Cable) and Rust (tokio broadcast). C++ (uWebSockets), Kotlin (Ktor), Scala and PHP (Laravel broadcasting via an external server) are thinner, and C is rare.

sources.supports: Fan-out across Node instances via Redis
Laravel broadcasting relies on an external WebSocket server
